content: 1. Progestin-only oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are a form of hormonal contraception that contains only progestin, without estrogen, and are used to prevent pregnancy. 2. Emergency contraceptive pills are medications taken after unprotected intercourse to prevent pregnancy, typically effective within a specific time frame. 3. Combined hormonal contraceptive patches deliver both estrogen and progestin through the skin to prevent ovulation and pregnancy. 4. Injectable contraceptives are long-acting hormonal methods administered via injection, typically effective for one to three months. 5. Contraceptive implants are small, flexible rods inserted under the skin that release progestin to prevent pregnancy for several years. 6. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are small, T-shaped devices inserted into the uterus to prevent pregnancy, available in hormonal and non-hormonal (copper) forms. 7. Female sterilization is a permanent method of contraception involving surgical procedures to block or seal the fallopian tubes. 8. Policies must ensure that all females of reproductive age have access to sexual and reproductive health services, the right to confidentiality, and freedom from discrimination in healthcare regardless of age. 9. Facilities should have written policies, standards, or guidelines based on national standards, which may include policy documents, standard operating procedures, or clinical practice guidelines. 10. Staff should be oriented to these policies, standards, or guidelines to ensure proper implementation. 11. Policies should also address the availability of medical abortion services, including access to medications at the primary level or through referral systems. 12. Family planning during emergencies should be prepared and implemented, ensuring access to methods such as IUDs and other modern contraceptives. 13. Facilities must review family planning clinic registers for women aged 15–49 or stock records from the previous 12 months to count the total number of modern contraceptive methods provided or prescribed. 14. The total number of methods provided or prescribed should be multiplied by a conversion factor to calculate the total couple-years of protection (CYP) for the previous 12 months by method. 15. The individual CYPs should be added to determine the total CYP provided. 16. Quantities of contraceptive methods such as pills, condoms, IUDs, implants, and injections administered, as well as sterilization operations performed, should be recorded. 17. The estimated protection provided by family planning services during a one-year period is calculated based on the volume of contraceptives distributed or sold. 18. Facilities should estimate the catchment population using census-based data and demographic surveys to determine the number of women eligible for modern contraceptive methods and the supplies needed for the next year. 19. Data from facility registers should be reviewed to validate reported data against facility records, ensuring accuracy and identifying discrepancies. 20. Staff training records should be reviewed to ensure that outpatient clinic staff working in infant and child health care have received appropriate training within the past five years. 21. Findings from staff training reviews should be summarized, including the total number of staff trained by category (e.g., doctors, nurses) and the proportion trained in specific topics. 22. Facilities should identify priority actions to improve family planning services by consolidating findings from checklists, identifying strengths and areas for improvement, and agreeing on key actions to address gaps. 23. Evaluation teams should synthesize findings from multiple facilities, using summary forms to record data and identify trends, strengths, and areas for improvement across different levels of healthcare facilities. 24. Monitoring and evaluation tables should be reviewed to track progress, identify indicators that are low or show no improvement, and prioritize areas for action. 25. Benchmarks for scale-up readiness should be reviewed annually to ensure progress and address gaps in family planning service delivery. 26. Communication plans should target high-risk women in subpopulations to improve access to family planning services. 27. Core interventions such as injectables, implants, IUDs, and sterilization should be prioritized to enhance family planning services. 28. Facilities should use summary forms to evaluate the percentage of health facility standards met and identify differences between levels of outpatient facilities, such as national hospitals, referral hospitals, and first-level facilities. 29. Data should be entered electronically using standard spreadsheet files to ensure accurate record-keeping and facilitate analysis. 30. Evaluation teams should discuss findings, reach consensus on main issues, and develop actionable plans to address identified gaps in family planning services.
